title: What is predicate pushdown — the Catalyst Optimizer pushes filter conditions down to the data source (Parquet/ORC/JDBC) so rows are filtered before being read into Spark memory — and why is it less effective with row-based formats (CSV/JSON must read full rows)?
shortTitle: Predicate pushdown — filtering at the data source before reading into Spark

s1_definition.profdef: Predicate pushdown is an optimization where the Catalyst Optimizer pushes a query's filter conditions down to the data source so that rows failing the filter are eliminated at the source, before they are ever read into Spark's executor memory. For columnar formats like Parquet and ORC, the source uses per-chunk statistics and encodings to skip whole row groups that cannot match; for JDBC sources, the predicate becomes a SQL WHERE clause executed by the database. It is less effective for row-based text formats like CSV and JSON because they have no column statistics, so Spark must read and parse every full row before applying the filter.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India's archive clerk. Without pushdown, the clerk hauls every box of records to your desk and you throw away the irrelevant ones yourself — exhausting. With predicate pushdown, you tell the clerk up front "only boxes for transactions above fifty thousand rupees," and the archive's own index lets the clerk leave the other boxes on the shelf. But if the archive is just loose unlabelled papers in a heap (CSV/JSON), there is no index, so the clerk still has to pick up and read every single sheet before deciding — the instruction helps far less.
s1_definition.oneliner: Predicate pushdown filters at the source before data enters Spark, saving I/O — powerful for columnar Parquet/ORC with statistics, weak for row-based CSV/JSON that must read every row.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Predicate pushdown is an optimization where the Catalyst Optimizer pushes a query's filter conditions down to the data source so that rows failing the filter are eliminated at the source, before they are ever read into Spark's executor memory. For columnar formats like Parquet and ORC, the source uses per-chunk statistics and encodings to skip whole row groups that cannot match; for JDBC sources, the predicate becomes a SQL WHERE clause executed by the database. It is less effective for row-based text formats like CSV and JSON because they have no column statistics, so Spark must read and parse every full row before applying the filter.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India's archive clerk. Without pushdown, the clerk hauls every box of records to your desk and you throw away the irrelevant ones yourself — exhausting. With predicate pushdown, you tell the clerk up front "only boxes for transactions above fifty thousand rupees," and the archive's own index lets the clerk leave the other boxes on the shelf. But if the archive is just loose unlabelled papers in a heap (CSV/JSON), there is no index, so the clerk still has to pick up and read every single sheet before deciding — the instruction helps far less.

**One line to remember:** Predicate pushdown filters at the source before data enters Spark, saving I/O — powerful for columnar Parquet/ORC with statistics, weak for row-based CSV/JSON that must read every row.

sections.s2_technical:
When you write a query like `spark.read.parquet(path).filter(col("amount") > 50000)`, Catalyst does not blindly read everything and then filter. It analyzes the filter and, if the data source supports it, hands the predicate to the source reader. This is predicate pushdown. The effect is that the source returns fewer rows, so less data crosses from storage into executor memory, which cuts I/O, network, and CPU for deserialization — usually the dominant costs in a scan.

For Parquet and ORC, the source has rich metadata. Each file is divided into row groups, and each column chunk in a row group stores min and max statistics. When the reader sees `amount > 50000`, it checks each row group's max for the amount column; if the max is below fifty thousand, no row in that group can match, so the whole group is skipped without decompressing it. ORC behaves similarly with its stripe-level statistics. This is why columnar formats make pushdown so effective: the statistics let the reader skip large blocks cheaply.

For JDBC sources, pushdown means Catalyst translates the Spark filter into a SQL WHERE clause sent to the database, so the database does the filtering and returns only matching rows. This is extremely effective because the database can use its own indexes. You can see this in the pushed filters section of the physical plan.

Row-based formats are the weak case. CSV and JSON store data row by row with no per-column statistics and no block-level min and max. So even if Spark pushes the predicate conceptually, the reader must still read, decompress, and parse each full row to evaluate the filter, because there is no way to skip ahead. The filter still reduces how many rows flow downstream, but it saves almost nothing on the expensive read-and-parse step. This is one of the strongest practical arguments for storing analytical data in Parquet or ORC rather than CSV or JSON.

A senior-level nuance is that pushdown only works for predicates the source understands — simple comparisons, equality, IN, and ranges on columns. A filter wrapped in a non-deterministic function or a user-defined function usually cannot be pushed down and runs in Spark after reading. You can verify pushdown by calling explain and reading the PushedFilters line on the scan node; filters listed there were pushed to the source, and filters shown as a separate Filter node ran in Spark.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India stores years of transactions and an analyst wants only high-value transfers above fifty thousand rupees. If the data is Parquet, the reader can skip entire row groups whose maximum amount is below the threshold, reading only the blocks that might contain matches. This is predicate pushdown with Parquet statistics.

Problem 2 — The same query against a CSV export of the data cannot skip anything, because CSV has no statistics, so every row is read and parsed before the filter applies. Comparing the two shows why format choice matters.

Problem 3 — A query against the live accounts database over JDBC pushes the filter into a SQL WHERE clause, so the database returns only matching rows using its index. This shows the JDBC form of pushdown.

The demo simulates row groups with min and max statistics for Parquet, a flat CSV with no statistics, and a JDBC source that applies the WHERE clause, then reports how many rows and bytes each actually reads for the same filter.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one million transactions in four Parquet row groups of 250,000 rows each, with amount ranges 100 to 9000, 10000 to 48000, 40000 to 120000, and 55000 to 900000; the same data as CSV; and the same data behind a JDBC database. The filter is amount greater than 50,000.

Step 1: For Parquet, the reader checks each row group's maximum amount. Group 0 maxes at 9000 and group 1 maxes at 48000, both below 50,000, so both are skipped entirely using the min and max statistics. Groups 2 and 3 might contain matches, so they are read — 500,000 of the million rows.

Step 2: For CSV, there are no statistics, so the reader must read and parse all one million rows before the filter can be evaluated. The filter reduces downstream rows but saves nothing on the read.

Step 3: For JDBC, the predicate becomes a SQL WHERE clause executed by the database using its index, so the database returns only the matching rows — about 300,000 — and Spark never sees the rest.

Step 4: The demo logs the rows read by each source, showing Parquet skipping half the data, CSV reading everything, and JDBC returning only matches.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 04:34:10 [INFO] Parquet (amount > 50000): read 500000 of 1000000 rows — row groups 0 and 1 skipped by min/max pushdown
2026-10-30 04:34:10 [WARNING] CSV (amount > 50000): read ALL 1000000 rows — no statistics, every row parsed before filtering
2026-10-30 04:34:10 [INFO] JDBC (amount > 50000): DB executed WHERE, returned only 300000 matching rows using its index
2026-10-30 04:34:10 [INFO] Pushdown is powerful with Parquet/JDBC and weak with CSV — store analytics data columnar.
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Query: filter(amount > 50000)
    │
    ├─ PARQUET source
    │    row group maxes: [9000][48000][120000][900000]
    │    skip RG0, RG1 (max < 50000)  → read RG2, RG3 only
    │    ▼ 500k rows into Spark
    │
    ├─ CSV source
    │    no stats → read+parse ALL rows
    │    ▼ 1,000k rows into Spark, then filter wasteful
    │
    ▼ JDBC source
       push WHERE amount > 50000 to DB (uses index)
       ▼ only 300k matching rows returned to Spark
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Predicate pushdown is the optimization where the Catalyst Optimizer pushes a query's filter conditions down to the data source so that rows failing the filter are eliminated before they ever enter Spark's executor memory. Because reading and deserializing data is usually the most expensive part of a scan, filtering at the source saves I/O, network, and CPU, and it is one of the most important performance behaviours to understand.

How well it works depends entirely on the source. For columnar formats like Parquet and ORC, each file is split into row groups, and every column chunk stores min and max statistics. When Spark pushes a filter like amount greater than fifty thousand, the reader checks each row group's maximum for that column, and if the maximum is below the threshold it skips the entire group without even decompressing it. For a JDBC source, the predicate is translated into a SQL WHERE clause that the database executes using its own indexes, returning only matching rows. Both are extremely effective.

Row-based text formats are the weak case, and this is the part interviewers want to hear. CSV and JSON have no per-column statistics and no block-level min and max, so even though Spark pushes the predicate conceptually, the reader still has to read, decompress, and parse every full row before it can evaluate the filter. The filter reduces how many rows flow downstream but saves almost nothing on the costly read-and-parse step. At the National Bank of India this was exactly why we stored our analytical transaction data in Parquet rather than CSV exports — a high-value-transfer query on Parquet skipped most of the data using min and max statistics, while the same query on the CSV copy read every single row. I verify pushdown actually happened by calling explain and reading the PushedFilters line on the scan, and my rule is that for analytics you store data columnar so predicate pushdown can do its job.
